t:
(a) Establishment.—The Commissioner and the Director shall establish and carry out on a fiscal year basis educational seminars to—
        (1) improve the ability of personnel of U.S. Customs and Border Protection to classify and appraise articles imported into the United States in accordance with the customs and trade laws of the United States; 
        (2) improve the trade enforcement efforts of personnel of U.S. Customs and Border Protection and personnel of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement; and 
        (3) otherwise improve the ability and effectiveness of personnel of U.S. Customs and Border Protection and personnel of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement to facilitate legitimate international trade.  
    (b) Content.—
        (1) Classifying and appraising imported articles.—In carrying out subsection (a)(1), the Commissioner, the Director, and interested parties in the private sector selected under subsection (c) shall provide instruction and related instructional materials at each educational seminar carried out under this section to personnel of U.S. Customs and Border Protection and, as appropriate, to personnel of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement on the following:
            (A) Conducting a physical inspection of an article imported into the United States, including testing of samples of the article, to determine if the article is mislabeled in the manifest or other accompanying documentation. 
            (B) Reviewing the manifest and other accompanying documentation of an article imported into the United States to determine if the country of origin of the article listed in the manifest or other accompanying documentation is accurate. 
            (C) Customs valuation. 
            (D) Industry supply chains and other related matters as determined to be appropriate by the Commissioner.  
        (2) Trade enforcement efforts.—In carrying out subsection (a)(2), the Commissioner, the Director, and interested parties in the private sector selected under subsection (c) shall provide instruction and related instructional materials at each educational seminar carried out under this section to personnel of U.S. Customs and Border Protection and, as appropriate, to personnel of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement to identify opportunities to enhance enforcement of the following:
            (A) Collection of countervailing duties assessed under subtitle A of title VII of the Tariff Act of 1930 (19 U.S.C. 1671 et seq.) and antidumping duties assessed under subtitle B of title VII of the Tariff Act of 1930 (19 U.S.C. 1673 et seq.). 
            (B) Addressing evasion of duties on imports of textiles. 
            (C) Protection of intellectual property rights. 
            (D) Enforcement of child labor laws.  
        (3) Approval of commissioner and director.—The instruction and related instructional materials at each educational seminar carried out under this section shall be subject to the approval of the Commissioner and the Director.  
    (c) Selection Process.—
        (1) In general.—The Commissioner shall establish a process to solicit, evaluate, and select interested parties in the private sector for purposes of assisting in providing instruction and related instructional materials described in subsection (b) at each educational seminar carried out under this section. 
        (2) Criteria.—The Commissioner shall evaluate and select interested parties in the private sector under the process established under paragraph (1) based on—
            (A) availability and usefulness; 
            (B) the volume, value, and incidence of mislabeling or misidentification of origin of imported articles; and 
            (C) other appropriate criteria established by the Commissioner.  
        (3) Public availability.—The Commissioner and the Director shall publish in the Federal Register a detailed description of the process established under paragraph (1) and the criteria established under paragraph (2).  
    (d) Special Rule for Antidumping and Countervailing Duty Orders.—
        (1) In general.—The Commissioner shall give due consideration to carrying out an educational seminar under this section in whole or in part to improve the ability of personnel of U.S. Customs and Border Protection to enforce a countervailing or antidumping duty order issued under section 706 or 736 of the Tariff Act of 1930 (19 U.S.C. 1671e or 1673e) upon the request of a petitioner in an action underlying such countervailing or antidumping duty order. 
        (2) Interested party.—A petitioner described in paragraph (1) shall be treated as an interested party in the private sector for purposes of the requirements of this section.  
    (e) Performance Standards.—The Commissioner and the Director shall establish performance standards to measure the 
development and level of achievement of educational seminars carried out under this section. 
    (f) Reporting.—Not later than September 30, 2016, and annually thereafter, the Commissioner and the Director shall submit to the appropriate congressional committees a report on the effectiveness of educational seminars carried out under this section. 
    (g) Definitions.—In this section:
        (1) Director.—The term “Director” means the Director of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. 
        (2) United states.—The term “United States” means the customs territory of the United States, as defined in General Note 2 to the Harmonized Tariff Schedule of the United States. 
        (3) U.S. customs and border protection personnel.—The term “U.S. Customs and Border Protection personnel” means import specialists, auditors, and other appropriate employees of the U.S. Customs and Border Protection. 
        (4) U.S. immigration and customs enforcement personnel.—The term “U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement personnel” means Homeland Security Investigations Directorate personnel and other appropriate employees of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

fable.w: The section requires the agencies to coordinate with selected private-sector parties, who jointly provide instruction to federal enforcement personnel on classification, supply chains and enforcement opportunities. It also requires the Commissioner to give due consideration to a private petitioner's request to hold a seminar, so outsiders feed into a federal decision. The tempting "No" reading is that this is only internal training, with the selection process resembling an application and the report going to Congress. That reading has real force, but the outside parties' role goes beyond applying: they help shape how federal personnel carry out trade enforcement.
fable.s: the Commissioner, the Director, and interested parties in the private sector selected under subsection (c) shall provide instruction and related instructional materials at each educational seminar carried out under this section to personnel of U.S. Customs and Border Protection

qwen_block.w: This section requires the federal government to solicit and select 'interested parties in the private sector' to participate in educational seminars by providing instruction. This involves coordination with outside entities (private sector companies/individuals) before the seminars are conducted, fitting the definition of participation. The tempting reading might be that this is just internal training, but the explicit requirement to select and involve private sector actors for instruction makes it participation.
qwen_block.s: The Commissioner shall establish a process to solicit, evaluate, and select interested parties in the private sector for purposes of assisting in providing instruction and related instructional materials described in subsection (b) at each educational seminar carried out under this section.

opus.w: Private-sector petitioners are outside the federal government, and they can request seminars that the Commissioner must give due consideration before deciding whether to hold one. Selected private-sector parties also help develop and deliver the seminar instruction, subject to agency approval, so outsiders contribute to agency decisions. The tempting 'No' reading treats this as purely internal staff training, as in the study-consultation example. But here outside parties' requests and input directly feed a federal decision about seminar content.
opus.s: The Commissioner shall give due consideration to carrying out an educational seminar under this section in whole or in part to improve the ability of personnel of U.S. Customs and Border Protection to enforce a countervailing or antidumping duty order issued under section 706 or 736 of the Tariff Act of 1930 (19 U.S.C. 1671e or 1673e) upon the request of a petitioner in an action underlying such countervailing or antidumping duty order.
opus.b:
I labeled this **Yes**, with moderate confidence (0.62).

**The tempting-but-wrong reading:** this section is mostly about training federal staff. The seminars teach Customs and Border Protection and Immigration and Customs Enforcement personnel. Publishing the selection process in the Federal Register is a notice, not a comment period or rulemaking. And private parties who teach are arguably delivering a service rather than shaping a decision. Example 3, where outside experts helped with a study, suggests "No" on that basis.

**Why I still chose Yes:** subsection (d) lets outsiders trigger a federal decision. A petitioner in an antidumping or countervailing duty case is a private company. It can request a seminar, and the Commissioner must give that request "due consideration" when deciding whether to hold one. Outside parties also help write the instructional materials alongside the agencies, subject to the agencies' approval. So people outside the government help decide what the agencies do.

qwen_chat.w: This section establishes an internal training program for federal employees. While private sector parties are selected to provide instruction, they are acting as instructors or consultants rather than participants in a decision-making process. The federal officials (Commissioner and Director) make the decisions regarding the seminars and approve the content; the private parties do not consult with the government before a decision is made, nor do they serve on an advisory board influencing policy. The interaction is operational (training) rather than participatory in the regulatory or decision-making sense defined.
qwen_chat.s: The Commissioner shall establish a process to solicit, evaluate, and select interested parties in the private sector for purposes of assisting in providing instruction and related instructional materials described in subsection (b) at each educational seminar carried out under this section.
qwen_chat.b:
Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that because private sector parties are selected to provide instruction, this constitutes "participation" in a federal decision. However, the definition explicitly excludes applications for benefits or grants, and more importantly, this section describes an internal training program for federal employees. The private parties are acting as instructors/consultants to improve the skills of federal personnel, not as participants in a decision-making process regarding a specific federal action, rule, or policy affecting the public. The "decision" here is the content of the training, which is approved by federal officials (Commissioner and Director), and the private parties are merely providing expertise. There is no consultation with outsiders *before* a federal decision that affects the outsiders' rights or obligations in the manner described (e.g., rulemaking, permitting, advisory boards on policy). The private parties are selected to *assist* in providing instruction, not to advise on a decision.

Wait, let's re-read the definition carefully. "Participation is when the federal government may or must consult or coordinate with people outside of the government before making a decision."
Does the government make a decision here? The government decides to hold seminars. The government selects private parties to help teach. Is the selection of private parties a "decision" that requires consultation? No, the Commissioner *selects* them.
Is there an advisory board? No.
Is there a public comment period? No.
Is there consultation with states/tribes? No.
Is there a right to sue? No.

The private parties are "interested parties in the private sector" selected to provide instruction. This is essentially contracting out or using experts for training. It is not "participation" in the sense of the definition (consultation/coordination before a decision). The decision to hold the seminar is made by the Commissioner/Director. The decision on content is approved by them. The private parties are implementers/instructors.

Therefore, the label is "No".
